$comment: B1.5c person normalization rules. Catalog-derived only: every rule is derived from movies.director string forms observed in the snapshot (scout §2.2). No external name data. The two prohibited forms are as important as the allowed ones: a bare surname must never be expanded, because expansion changes the answer set (Q17: 'Steven Spielberg' = 5 rows vs 'Spielberg' = 29 rows).
source: fabflix-mysql:3307/moviedb movies.director (10,888 distinct strings; 788 'X.Lastname' abbreviations; 30 strings containing '~'; 1,398 surnames with more than one string)

semantics.equality: two director strings denote the same person only when the normalized surnames match AND, if either side carries a first initial or first name, the initials match.
semantics.recall_only: a bare surname may widen a candidate list for display/recall, never an answer-set comparison (docs/plans/b1-5c-tool-routing-fixes.md §5.4).
semantics.result_constraints_director: result_constraints.director is judged with the equality rule below; a bare surname is NOT a match for a full name.

rules.transform: replace '~' with a single space before any other step
rules.why: '~' is the catalog's space substitute; any split-on-space normalization fails without it (30 strings)

rules.transform: strip and collapse runs of whitespace to one space
'X.Lastname' equals 'First Last' only when the surname matches and the first initial matches
rules.counter_example: Ant.Mann != Michael Mann (initial A vs M)
rules.why: 788 abbreviated strings exist; the initial check blocks the surname collision families (58 strings contain 'Mann')

rules.transform: a bare surname is never expanded to a full name, and a full name is never reduced to 'any movie by someone with that surname'
rules.counter_example: Spielberg == Spielberg (identical strings are always equal)
rules.why: expansion enlarges the answer set (5 vs 29 rows for Q17) and cannot be justified from the query text

exceptions.description: when a surname has exactly one distinct director string in the catalog, equality holds by string identity, not by expansion
exceptions.example: Hitchcock (83 rows, one string) and Vertigo's director 'Hitchcock'
exceptions.note: this is not an exception to the prohibition: the strings ARE identical

assertions.sql_left: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies WHERE director = 'Steven Spielberg'
assertions.sql_right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies WHERE director = 'Spielberg'
assertions.explanation: Q17's golden answer set is the 5 rows of 'Steven Spielberg'. Treating the 29 'Spielberg' rows as equivalent would replace the answer set; B15c-6 therefore asserts 5 vs 29 and equal = false.
same surname 'mann', same first initial 'm' -> the abbreviation is the same person; both row counts stay separate only because the catalog stores two spellings.
'Mann' alone matches no catalog string in this snapshot, and even when a surname does match rows it is never a substitute for the full name.

notes: Q17 in docs/ai/golden/queries.b1-5.json uses 'Steven Spielberg' = 5 rows; the bare surname 'Spielberg' = 29 rows is a different set (scout §2.2, §3.3). Normalization must not change the answer set, which is exactly what a surname expansion would do.
1,398 surnames own more than one distinct string (lee 44, kim 26, smith 26, ...), so surname-only matching would merge unrelated people.

Chinese transliterations of director names (e.g. 希区柯克) are NOT normalized here: they are not derivable from the catalog. Under C4=D the query-time title resolver only resolves titles; a transliterated director stays a recall/display problem and must not be silently mapped.
